title: Closed doors
hook: at a conference by a lake, nations refuse refugees; a ship full of Jewish families is turned away

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kindertransport, and your line: the children went alone. Did a child at a school gate or a bus stop bring those platforms back? Today, the doors that didn't open, for the parents and for so many others. Day one thousand ten.

Where do you go when nobody will let you in? A grand hotel on the shore of a lake in France. Delegates from many countries arrive in good suits. There are speeches, dinners, walks by the water. They have come to talk about Jews trying to get out of Germany and Austria. Delegate after delegate stands up, expresses sympathy, and explains why their own country cannot take more. The meeting ends. The visas don't come. Today's word is what people trying to escape kept finding.
screen: `A HOTEL BY A LAKE.` → `SPEECH AFTER SPEECH OF SYMPATHY.` → `NO VISAS.`

segments.voice: The town was Evian, and the year was 1938. The conference there is remembered for what it did not do. Countries spoke of quotas, of jobs, of their own troubles at home. Very few doors opened. For Jews in Germany and Austria, the problem was no longer only getting out. It was finding anywhere that would let them in. The next year, a ship called the St. Louis sailed from Germany carrying Jewish refugees, families who had sold what they could to buy passage and landing papers for Cuba. When the ship reached Havana, the papers were declared no good, and most of the passengers were not allowed to land. The ship sailed on, close enough to the coast of the United States to see it, and asked to be let in there. The answer was no. Canada said no too. The St. Louis turned around and sailed back across the ocean. In the end, several European countries took the passengers in. Some of them were later caught when the war reached those countries, and did not survive. Closed doors were not only walls and guards. They were forms, quotas, and polite refusals in good suits. The Torah has a command that speaks to it. "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The command rests on memory: you know what it is to be the one outside. Jewish tradition keeps returning to the stranger, the person at the door with nowhere else to go. This chapter is part of why.
screen: `EVIAN: SYMPATHY, BUT NO VISAS.` · `THE ST. LOUIS AT HAVANA.` · `TURNED AWAY, SAILING BACK.` · `REFUSALS IN GOOD SUITS.` · then, large: `LOVE YE THEREFORE THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: open one door for someone. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who is on the outside of something right now. A newcomer at work. A neighbor who doesn't know anyone. Someone looking for a job, a room, a seat at the table. Stay with them for a moment, without fixing anything. Then let one small opening take shape: an introduction, an invitation, a reference, a chair pulled out. Something you could actually do. Hold it until the bell, and if you can, open it today. The bell holds the time.
Closed doors. The refusals at Evian, the ship turned away from Havana and from North America: the countries that would not let Jewish refugees in. Today's word.
Your line: doors closed. Today, when it is in your power to let someone in, to a conversation, a group, a line, let them in. Day one thousand ten.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching returns often to the command to love the stranger, and some Jewish refugee organizations today point to this history when they help refugees from anywhere.

original.note: Hebrew: the stranger, the one who lives among a people not their own. the Torah asks again and again that the ger be loved.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Jews of Europe could simply have left.
what it means: closed doors. at Evian and at Havana, doors stayed shut.
what a scholar hears: refusal by paper, quotas and polite speeches, set against a Torah that grounds love of the stranger in memory.
